newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia military calls for bigger "oil army".
newsitem.headline: Colombia military calls for bigger "oil army".

text.p: Colombia's army chief said on Thursday he needed 20,000 more soldiers to protect key oil infrastructure after a spate of leftist rebel attacks.
Speaking at an agricultural forum, Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett said more than 11,000 of the army's active fighting force of 80,000 men were already tied up protecting oil fields and pipelines.

"We must make an effort to boost the army's fighting force in (eastern) Casanare province. We cannot afford to move a single soldier out of that region," he said, referring to the oil-rich eastern plains region.

Casanare is the centre of British Petroleum Co Plc's Colombian operations, part of which ground to a halt for three weeks in June following threats to construction contractors from the National Liberation Army (ELN), the country's second-largest rebel force.
"I'm not going to protect just BP, I'm going to protect the oil of all Colombians," Bonett said.
His call for more troops came on the day that 20 soldiers, who died in an ELN attack in eastern Arauca province over the weekend, were buried in Bogota.

The rebels blew up a pipeline, which pumps crude from the Cano Limon field operated by U.S. multinational Occidental Petroleum Corp early on Sunday. They then shot down a helicopter in which the soldiers were travelling to the blast site.

Thursday's burial -- which was described by army officials as a symbolic funeral because the charred remains of the soldiers have not yet been fully identified -- was attended by President Ernesto Samper and armed forces chief Gen. Harold Bedoya. Once forensic tests have been completed, the soldiers will be reburied with personalized headstones.

Rebel attacks against key oil facilities have increased dramatically this year. The pipeline that runs from Cano Limon to the Caribbean coast port of Covenas has been dynamited 37 times so far this year, with the latest attack early on Thursday. It was hit 45 times in 1996, officials at the state-run oil company Ecopetrol say.

The Cuban-inspired ELN was set up by radical Roman Catholic priests in 1966 and specialises in attacks against the country's oil infrastructure. Oil has replaced coffee as Colombia's top export earner.
